# Summary {#part-ecosystem-summary .unnumbered}

Part XI examined the conditions under which the technical stack is supplied and used: model releases and artifacts, tooling, compute prices, market structure, adoption, data rights, and agent payments. Whether a model is offered through an API, as open weights, or under a restrictive license changes what builders can operate. The tooling standards, gateways, sandboxes, and observability around it shape which practices become common, and the cost of training and serving, measured per accepted result for a stated workload and time horizon, limits which designs a team can sustain.

Across these chapters, non-technical terms can act as technical constraints. Pricing, supply concentration, license terms, compliance duties, and rights claims can constrain an architecture as much as a benchmark result or a kernel's performance. Benchmark strength, access terms, serving cost, and the safeguard and rights work that an open release leaves to its deployer vary independently. A model can meet a product's requirement on one of them and fail it on another.

The ecosystem is one mechanism by which capability becomes access, lock-in, margin, and operational risk. The part leaves open how value will be divided among silicon suppliers, clouds, model providers, application companies, workers, and data rights holders if capability keeps becoming easier to rent. Part XII turns those market constraints into operating contracts: once a team buys or hosts capability, it has to run releases, budgets, tenant boundaries, incidents, and human approvals. A team that trains its own models also runs the stack that produces them, from the data manifest to the release gate.
